title: Interfacial solar evaporation: An up‐to‐date (2024–2025) review of materials, structures, and system designs for next‐generation desalination
content:
Abstract

Through this comprehensive 2024–2025 review, the recent trends in interfacial solar evaporation (ISE) systems are systematically analyzed, classifying progress into a number of themes including material innovation, structural engineering (2D–3D evolution and Janus/multi-surface designs), system integration, and theoretical interpretation, thus consolidating the overall proof for performance-relevant mechanisms and design trajectories. The results indicate considerable advancement in performance and operational robustness across the studied themes. These include solar-to-vapor conversion efficacies of more than 97% under one-sun illumination; rapid evaporation rates attaining between 1.4 and 2.2 kg/m2 h for standard seawater, with 3D architectures promoting an evaporation rate to 3.35 kg/m2 h (and beyond 3.61 kg/m2 h, which exceeds the performance ceiling of conventional 2D systems). Specifically, salt management has been improved via 2D–3D evolution, Janus configurations, and multi-surface engineering, permitting sustained operation in highly concentrated brines (20–25 wt % NaCl) for 10–24 h without measurable performance decay. Moreover, ISE reliably generates potable-quality water with ion and heavy-metal declines of 3–4 orders of magnitude, characteristically attaining TDS < 10 mg/L, well lower than WHO drinking water thresholds. Several next-generation designs; particularly novel structural architectures and hydrogel-based systems have reported excellent salt and heavy metal ions rejection of 99% and 99.9%, respectively, and even established salt harvesting of 26.7 g within 15 operational days. Long-term durability is also well reinforced, with stable operation beyond 15–28 days without self-cleansers and salt-rejection systems.
